opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is amply clear that neither the order dated 26.09.2008 nor the letter vide which the respondent was asked to give a presentation in any way restrained the respondent from completing the Variables.
There is no letter or correspondence by the respondent prior to 31.01.2009 wherein it has objected to the Government for not complying with its part of the obligations under the Agreement.
The delay in completing the Variables is thus solely on account of shortcoming or default on the part of the respondent.
38.
It is true that this Court cannot sit and act as an Appellate Court on the order passed by the Arbitrator, but where (36 of 46) [CMA-1454/2022] the provision of the Agreement has been by-passed and has been overlooked by the Tribunal, this Court is competent to look into the same.
There is no justification for the respondent in not completing the Variables by 31.01.2009 and there is no evidence that the Government of Rajasthan restrained or in any way created hindrance in completion of the Variables,
39. Since Variables 1, 2 and 3 were not completed, the Operate Part i.e. Variable 4 also did not commence.
The claimant has raised his claim under the head of capital expenditure, holding cost,
interest and legal cost.
It is evident that the term 'capital expenditure' and 'holding cost' is alien to the Agreement and the same are nowhere mentioned in the entire Agreement.
, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.
74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for.--1
41. Learned Tribunal has invoked the provisions of the Contract Act to compensate the respondent.
Learned Tribunal has erred in applying Section 73 of the Contract Act, since Section 73 of the Contract Act can be applied for the breach of the Contract when liquidated damages are not contemplated.
In the present case, the parties had already contemplated the liquidated damages, in the event of default by either side i.e. if there was a default on the part of the Government of Rajasthan, the Government of Rajasthan was to acquire the assets at 120% of the book value and if there was default on the part of the IL&FS, the Government of Rajasthan was to acquire the assets at the book value of 75%.
Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act stipulates that compensation for breach of Contract where penalty is (39 of 46) [CMA-1454/2022] stipulated for cannot exceed the amount so mentioned or as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.
46. The claim for organizing the enrolment camps is thus outside the scope of the Agreement and the learned Tribunal has clearly ignored the terms of the Agreement and has passed an award, (41 of 46) [CMA-1454/2022] which is opposed to public policy, more particularly since in the Agreement,
it was specifically mentioned that in case of any default of breach on the part of the Government of Rajasthan, the maximum amount which the respondent could have claimed was 120% of the book value of the assets.
There is no provision of claiming compensation for holding of the camps etc.
Thus, the award is opposed to the public policy.
It is true that none of the parties has terminated the Agreement, but assuming that the Agreement was terminated by the Government of Rajasthan on account of breach of IL&FS in (43 of 46) [CMA-1454/2022] completing Variables 1, 2 and 3, the maximum amount, which IL&FS would have taken from the Government of Rajasthan, was 75% of the book value of the assets and assuming that the Contract could not be completed because of default of the Government of Rajasthan, the maximum amount that IL&FS would have taken from the Government of Rajasthan was 120% of the book value of the assets.
There is no question of grant of any amount over and above that which was agreed to between the parties as liquidated damages in the Agreement as stipulated in Section 74 of Indian Contract Act.
51. We are of the considered view that the learned Arbitrator has erred in considering the case as breach of Government of Rajasthan rather, it is clearly a case of breach by IL&FS, as IL&FS has not completed the three Variables within the prescribed time and the time extended by the Government of Rajasthan.
Had IL&FS completed Variables 1, 2 and 3, it would have started receiving quarterly guaranteed payment from the Government of Rajasthan.
It is an admitted case of the respondent that it had not completed the Variables in time.
Its allegation that it was on account of Government of Rajasthan cannot be said to be true as there is no correspondence whatsoever on the part of IL&FS with regard to the breach on the part of the Government of Rajasthan.
It is only after the constitution of the Ministerial Committee that IL&FS has made a ground that delay in implementation of the project was on account of the Government of Rajasthan.
Since the build component was not completed, the operational period could not commence and therefore, IL&FS was in default in performance of its part of the Contract.
Learned Tribunal (45 of 46)
[CMA-1454/2022] has further held that in the overall facts and circumstances, in the considered opinion of the Tribunal, the claimant-respondent cannot be held guilty of any Event of Default or Material Breach as defined under the Agreement and it is the appellant, which is responsible for such Material Breach resulting in Material Adverse Effect.
Since the Tribunal has come to the conclusion that there is material breach resulting in Material Adverse Effect and that is on account of breach of the Government of Rajasthan, the maximum claim that the claimant-respondent was entitled to, was under Article 7 of the Agreement.
The learned Tribunal has clearly erred in holding that though mechanism for claiming termination and damages is provided under Article 7 of the Agreement, it is not a mandatory pre-requisite to lodge claims.
Learned Tribunal has further erred in awarding claim under Section 73 of the Contract Act when the Agreement itself provided for the liquidated damages and claims.
It is true that if the reasoning of the learned Arbitrator is to be countenanced, all the agreements would become non est and otiose and all the claimants would claim direct access to the Contract Act without paying heed to the agreement.
54.
The award passed by the learned Arbitrator saddled Government of Rajasthan with a huge cost,
despite there being a default on the part of the IL&FS.
Moreover, the award has been passed by going beyond the four corners of the Agreement.
Further, in view of Section 34(b)(ii) of the Act of 1996 read with Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act and above considered judgments, the arbitral award being in conflict with fundamental policy of Indian Law deserves to be set aside.
